subject: Paediatrics
summary: Neonatal jaundice is excess bilirubin in a newborn, usually benign but can progress to kernicterus if untreated. Clinicians must assess severity, identify cause, and initiate timely phototherapy or exchange transfusion.

sections.p: Jaundice is visible yellowing of skin and sclera due to unconjugated bilirubin. Diagnosis is clinical plus serum total bilirubin (TB) and direct fraction. A TB >15 mg/dL in a term infant warrants treatment.
b: Serum TB >15 mg/dL in term newborn

t.b: Measures bilirubin load; high levels predict risk of neurotoxicity
Differentiates hepatic vs hemolytic causes; >1.0 mg/dL suggests hepatic dysfunction

sections.p: The Bhutani nomogram stratifies risk by age in hours and TB. Low risk (<10 mg/dL at 24 h), moderate (10–15 mg/dL), high (>15 mg/dL).

t.b: Predicts need for phototherapy; high values trigger treatment

sections.p: In term infants, physiologic immaturity of UDP‑glucuronosyltransferase is common. Pathologic causes include hemolysis, infection, G6PD deficiency, ABO incompatibility, sepsis, and biliary atresia.

t.b: Detects spherocytes or schistocytes indicating hemolysis

sections.p: Early‑onset (within 24 h) jaundice suggests hemolysis or infection. Late‑onset (after 48 h) points to biliary atresia or sepsis. Phototherapy is started when TB exceeds risk thresholds.
Baseline labs guide etiology and monitor therapy. In low‑resource settings, point‑of‑care bilirubin and hemoglobin are essential.

t.b: Assesses anemia and reticulocytosis; high retics suggest hemolysis
Positive indicates immune hemolysis; negative suggests non‑immune causes
Elevated ALT/AST point to hepatic injury

sections.p: Kernicterus, acute bilirubin encephalopathy, and death are the most feared complications. Prompt treatment prevents them.

t.b: Detects early signs of bilirubin encephalopathy

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first. Phototherapy is first‑line for moderate cases; exchange transfusion is reserved for severe or refractory jaundice. Supportive care includes hydration and monitoring.

t.b: Higher intensity lowers bilirubin faster; monitor skin temperature to avoid overheating

sections.p: Re‑check TB 48–72 h after treatment. Counsel parents on breastfeeding, early feeding, and avoiding delayed cord clamping. Screen for hemolytic disease in subsequent pregnancies.
Physiologic jaundice, neonatal sepsis, and congenital hypothyroidism can mimic or coexist with jaundice.
Low bilirubin in a sick infant may be due to hemolysis masking high total bilirubin. Point‑of‑care devices can underestimate TB in dark‑skinned babies.
b: Dark skin pigmentation may reduce accuracy of visual assessment

whenToSeekHelp: Severe jaundice (TB >20 mg/dL), rapid rise in bilirubin, lethargy, poor feeding, seizures, or any sign of neurologic dysfunction

faq.a: When TB exceeds the age‑specific risk threshold on the Bhutani nomogram or is >15 mg/dL in a term infant.
Breastfeeding itself does not worsen jaundice; inadequate intake can delay clearance, so frequent feeds are encouraged.
A severe neurotoxicity where unconjugated bilirubin deposits in the brain, leading to permanent neurologic damage.
